1.name: Housing half
1.note: The flame-retardant case. The two halves enclose the mechanism and insulate it from the user.

2.name: DIN rail clip
2.note: Snaps the breaker onto a DIN rail in the panel.

3.name: Terminal cage
3.note: Clamps the incoming and outgoing conductors against the strips.

4.name: Screw
4.note: Tightens the terminal cage onto the conductor.

5.name: Line strip, upper runner
5.note: Carries the supply from the line terminal to the fixed contact.

6.name: Fixed contact tip
6.note: The silver-graphite contact the moving tip closes on. Graphite resists welding when the arc strikes at opening.

7.name: Lower arc runner
7.note: Gives the arc a path to climb into the arc chute when the contacts part.

8.name: Splitter plate
8.note: The arc chute. It splits the arc into short arcs in series, raising its voltage until the current dies.

9.name: Coil lead strip
9.note: Carries the current on to the solenoid coil.

10.name: Moving contact arm
10.note: Swings on the main pivot to open and close the circuit. It is the switch that the pattern's closed and open states describe.

11.name: Moving contact tip
11.note: The silver-nickel tip on the arm. It meets the fixed tip when the breaker is closed.

12.name: Main pivot pin
12.note: The shared pivot for the contact arm and the cradle.

13.name: Cradle
13.note: Links the handle to the contact arm. The pawl holds it, so freeing the latch lets the arm spring open whatever the handle does.

14.name: Latch pawl
14.note: Holds the cradle against the arm spring. A knock from the trip lever releases it and the breaker trips open.

15.name: Trip lever
15.note: Takes the push from the bimetal or the striker and knocks the pawl out of the latch.

16.name: Coupling link
16.note: Connects the handle crank to the cradle.

17.name: Toggle handle
17.note: The switch and reset. After a trip it holds a reset only once the bimetal has cooled enough: open, then half-open, then closed.

18.name: Handle pin
18.note: The pivot of the toggle handle.

19.name: Handle spring
19.note: Acts on the handle so that it settles at the end of its travel.

20.name: Arm spring
20.note: Drives the contact arm open as soon as the latch lets go, and keeps the contacts pressed together when closed.

21.name: Solenoid coil
21.note: The magnetic trip. It carries the load current, so a short circuit pulls the plunger at once, with no waiting.

22.name: Coil former
22.note: The bobbin the coil is wound on. It insulates the windings from the plunger.

23.name: Magnet yoke with core
23.note: Guides the coil's magnetic flux into the plunger across the air gap.

24.name: Plunger
24.note: Pulled in by the coil above the magnetic threshold. It drives the striker onto the trip lever.

25.name: Striker pin
25.note: Carries the plunger's blow to the trip lever.

26.name: Plunger spring
26.note: Holds the plunger back. Its preload sets the current at which the magnetic trip acts.

27.name: Flexible braid
27.note: Flexible leads that carry current to the moving arm and the bimetal without hindering their movement.

28.name: Bimetal
28.note: The thermal trip. Heated by its own current, an overload bends it until it knocks the latch out; the higher the current, the sooner.

29.name: Load strip
29.note: Carries the current from the bimetal to the load terminal.

30.name: Set screw
30.note: Calibration screw. It sets the gap before the bimetal's tip touches the trip lever, and so how long the thermal trip takes.
